description: We are a multidisciplinary team of engineering students interested in aerospace, robotics, AI/ML, data science, and space technology. We are motivated team members with complementary skills in software development, data analysis, GIS/remote sensing, UI/UX, research, and science. We want to combine technical expertise with creativity and problem-solving to build an impactful solution for the NASA Space Apps Challenge.
summary:
SkyShift is a web tool built on NASA's SPHEREx data that lets users look up regions of the sky using RA/Dec coordinates or by searching for a specific space object. It presents observations of the selected region, captured at different points in time, as an interactive flipbook, allowing users to track changes in the sky easily. Image processing involves image alignment, inverse-variance weighted stacking and image subtraction to create clean, comparable SPHEREx images across different visits, thus reducing noise and positional errors to make changes and moving-object detection more reliable.
Our project also includes accessibility features such as voice interaction, text-to-speech sonification, keyboard navigation, and screen-reader support.
details:
SKYSHIFT

SKYSHIFT is an interactive astronomy platform built around NASA's SPHEREx mission. It allows users to explore infrared observations of the sky, identify objects that move or change over time, and investigate potential astronomical discoveries using real scientific data.

1. What does SKYSHIFT do?

NASA's SPHEREx photographs the entire sky every six months in 102 infrared colours. Our project SKYSHIFT turns these observations into an interactive experience where users can:

  • Explore the sky: Search for objects by name or coordinates, or select regions using an interactive sky map.
  • Watch the sky change: View observations as a time-based flipbook to spot moving objects and changes in brightness.
  • Find unusual objects: Detect potential moving objects, variable stars and transient events.
  • Study infrared data: Explore all 102 spectral bands, compare observations and examine spectral features.
  • Investigate discoveries: View object information, measurements, motion data and possible explanations.

2. How does it work?

  • Retrieves SPHEREx observations from NASA's IRSA archive for a selected region.
  • Aligns and processes images from different observation periods.
  • Uses image comparison and automated detection to identify objects that move or change.
  • Analyses brightness variations, motion and spectral features.
  • Cross-checks detected objects against existing astronomical catalogues to distinguish new candidates from known objects.

For verification, SKYSHIFT uses:

  • Gaia DR3: Stellar positions, distances and proper motion.
  • SIMBAD: Existing object identifications and classifications.
  • 2MASS and AllWISE: Infrared observations and photometric information.
  • IMCCE SkyBoT: Known asteroids and other solar-system objects.
  • NASA Exoplanet Archive: Connections between stars and known planetary systems.

3. What makes SKYSHIFT creative?

We wanted to go beyond displaying astronomical images and find more engaging ways to explore the data.

Some of the features include:

  • Time-based flipbook: Plays observations from different dates in sequence, making movement and brightness changes easier to spot.
  • 102-colour spectral cube: A 3D visualisation that lets users explore SPHEREx's infrared bands.
  • Colour-by-date view: Assigns different colours to observations from different dates, making moving objects appear as coloured trails.
  • Time Machine: Combines historical photographic plates with modern observations to trace how objects have moved across decades.
  • Asteroid Hunter: Helps identify and investigate known solar-system objects.
  • Molecule and mineral feature finder: Examines spectral features that may indicate the presence of particular molecules or materials.
  • Discovery Board: Allows users to report potential discoveries, share findings and vote on interesting candidates.
  • Technical reports: Users can generate reports containing measurements and analysis for further investigation.

4. Accessibility and inclusivity

Making astronomy accessible to people with different abilities and levels of experience was an important consideration.

  • Listen mode: Designed for blind and low-vision users, with spoken descriptions, voice interaction and spatial audio.
  • Sonification: Translates visual information into sound. Brightness changes can be heard, while object movement can be represented through audio moving between the left and right ears.
  • Simple and Expert modes: Simple mode uses plain-language explanations and guided exploration, while Expert mode provides detailed scientific tools and measurements.
  • Guided tour: Introduces new users to the platform and its features.
  • Keyboard and screen-reader support: Helps users navigate and interact with the application without relying entirely on a mouse or visual interface.

5. Tools and technologies

    • React
    • Vite
    • JavaScript
    • Python
    • FastAPI
    • Numpy
    • Astropy
    • Pillow
    • Chart.js
    • Aladin Lite
    • NASA IRSA
    • Gaia DR3
    • SIMBAD
    • 2MASS
    • AllWISE
    • SkyBot
    • NASA Exoplanet Archive
    • Oracle Cloud

6. Performance and data handling

Astronomical datasets can be large and take considerable time to download and process. We addressed this through:

  • Background download jobs with progress indicators.
  • Cancellation controls for ongoing requests.
  • Local caching of downloaded and processed datasets, so previously explored regions can load much faster.
  • Pre-downloading frequently used regions to make demonstrations and repeat visits faster.
  • Periodic checks for new SPHEREx data releases so cached observations can be updated.

7. Intended impact

SKYSHIFT aims to make real astronomical data more accessible, understandable and engaging.

We hope it can be useful to:

  • Students and educators looking for interactive ways to learn astronomy.
  • Amateur astronomers and citizen scientists interested in exploring real telescope observations.
  • Researchers who want to investigate candidate objects and compare observations with existing catalogues.
  • People with visual impairments who are often left out of astronomy tools that rely heavily on images.

By combining scientific analysis, interactive visualisation, sound-based exploration and accessible explanations, SKYSHIFT makes it possible for more people to participate in exploring the universe.

The project will be open source, allowing others to explore the code, use its documented API and build upon the work.
